# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: Promise, Pitfalls, and a Path Forward

## Introduction and rationale

Permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES) have transformed percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), but the enduring presence of a rigid metal cage has been implicated in late adverse events including very late stent thrombosis, neoatherosclerosis, impaired vasomotion, and exclusion of future surgical or percutaneous options. In patients who receive metallic drug-eluting coronary stents, adverse events such as late target-lesion failure may be related in part to the persistent presence of the metallic stent frame in the coronary-vessel wall, and bioresorbable vascular scaffolds have been developed to attempt to improve long-term outcomes. The conceptual appeal of bioresorbable scaffolds (BRS) lies in providing transient mechanical support and antiproliferative drug delivery during the early healing phase, after which complete resorption restores vascular structure and function [1,2].

## Early devices and first-in-human experience

Two principal material strategies emerged: bioresorbable polymers and bioresorbable metal alloys. The first clinical use of a fully absorbable metal device came with magnesium. In the PROGRESS-AMS trial, Erbel and colleagues evaluated temporary scaffolding of coronary arteries with bioabsorbable magnesium stents in a prospective, non-randomised multicentre study. The polymeric platform that came to dominate the field was the everolimus-eluting poly-L-lactide Absorb scaffold. Ormiston and colleagues reported a bioabsorbable everolimus-eluting coronary stent system for patients with single de-novo coronary artery lesions (ABSORB) in a prospective open-label trial [3], with 2-year multimodality imaging follow-up subsequently confirming feasibility [4]. The Absorb scaffold consists of a 150-μm-thick bioresorbable poly(l-lactide) scaffold with a 7-μm-thick bioresorbable poly(d,l-lactide) coating, which elutes everolimus.

## Randomized trial evidence

The pivotal randomized trials compared Absorb against the cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting Xience stent. In the large, multicenter ABSORB III trial, 2008 patients with stable or unstable angina were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive an everolimus-eluting bioresorbable vascular (Absorb) scaffold [5]. The ABSORB II trial assessed mechanistic endpoints but was disappointing: it did not meet its co-primary endpoints of superior vasomotor reactivity and non-inferior late luminal loss for the Absorb scaffold relative to the metallic stent, and a higher rate of device-oriented composite endpoint due to target vessel myocardial infarction was observed in the Absorb group [6]. A patient-level pooled meta-analysis showed broadly comparable 1-year efficacy [7], but a concerning safety signal soon emerged. Patients treated with a bioresorbable vascular scaffold had an increased risk of subacute stent thrombosis [8]. The all-comers AIDA trial reinforced this: treatment with the bioresorbable scaffold was associated with a significantly higher incidence of overall and very late device thrombosis than was the metallic stent through 2 years of follow-up [9], with concordant findings at 5 years [10]. The 2-year pooled analysis of seven trials similarly documented excess events [11], as did the high-risk COMPARE-ABSORB trial, in which enrolment was discontinued prematurely because of a high thrombosis and target vessel myocardial infarction rate in the BVS arm [12].

## The 3-year inflection point

A consistent theme is that excess risk is concentrated during the period before complete resorption. BVS compared with cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents resulted in higher 3-year rates of target lesion failure (11.7% versus 8.1%), driven by greater target vessel myocardial infarction [13]. The final ABSORB program report quantified this: between 0 and 5 years, target lesion failure occurred in 15.9% of BVS patients versus 13.1% of EES patients, and device thrombosis occurred in 2.2% versus 1.0% [14]. In ABSORB III, cumulative 5-year adverse event rates were increased after BVS compared with everolimus-eluting stents; however, the period of excess risk ended at 3 years, coincident with complete scaffold resorption [15]. Network and time-varying meta-analyses corroborate the elevated very late thrombosis hazard [16,17,18], and even five-year registry data show that the thrombotic signal attenuates after the resorption window [19,20].

## Mechanisms and implantation technique

Mechanistic studies attributed early thrombosis and myocardial infarction partly to thick struts, limited radial strength, and suboptimal deployment. The higher scaffold thrombosis rates observed with first-generation BRS compared to conventional DES were likely due in part to bioresorbable polymers having insufficient radial strength, necessitating larger strut profiles [21]. This motivated emphasis on predilatation, sizing, and postdilatation technique [22,23]. The blinded ABSORB IV trial applied optimised technique: polymeric BVS implanted with optimised technique in an expanded patient population resulted in non-inferior 30-day and 1-year rates of target lesion failure and angina compared with metallic DES [24], with a markedly lower 1-year scaffold thrombosis rate [25]. Acute coronary syndromes and small vessels remain higher-risk settings [26,27].

## Next-generation devices and outlook

Following commercial withdrawal of Absorb, attention shifted to thinner, stronger platforms, particularly resorbable magnesium scaffolds. BIOMAG-I reported outcomes of the new-generation sirolimus-eluting bioresorbable magnesium scaffold DREAMS 3G, showing low angiographic in-scaffold late lumen loss and excellent clinical safety and efficacy at 1 year [28], building on the DREAMS/BIOSOLVE programme [29,30]. Whether iterative engineering can deliver the long-term vascular restoration originally envisioned, without an early excess of thrombotic events, remains the central question for the field.
